Rating cuts were reversed when exams did not show real improvement.
A negative VA opinion built only on missing treatment records was ruled inadequate
Credible reports of an in-service injury and back pain since then supported the link.

helped.text: VA opinions were found inadequate or weak when they ignored the veteran's knee pain history.
Veteran's account of knee pain starting in service was found credible despite thin records.
Positive knee opinions that explained their reasons and used the veteran's history carried high weight.
Secondary knee claims were granted when the Board found a VA link opinion flawed.
Higher knee motion ratings followed documented pain-limited or flare-up motion.
Exams that skipped flare-up estimates or weight-bearing measurements were found inadequate.
A VA opinion resting on missing records, ignoring the veteran's account, was found inadequate.

hurt.text: Measured knee motion stayed well short of the next level, even counting pain and flare-ups.
Pain and flare-ups were found already covered by the current rating.
Silent service records and knee problems denied at exams weighed against the claim.
Later accounts of knee pain since service were outweighed by earlier histories and long gaps.
No current knee diagnosis, or normal exam findings, meant no disability for service connection.
Pain was already counted in the current rating, with no proof it limited motion further.
Private findings that were an outlier, or showed only where pain began, were set aside.

helped.text: A believable account that ringing began in service was accepted as evidence of onset.
A negative VA opinion lost weight when it leaned on silent service records.
Noise exposure accepted from the veteran's job met the in-service requirement.
Ringing that began within a year of discharge was accepted when described credibly
A VA opinion built on a wrong fact or another veteran's records lost weight.

hurt.text: The veteran's own reports placed the start of ringing years after leaving service.
A VA opinion that reviewed the file and gave reasons was trusted
The veteran's own view that service caused the ringing was not accepted
Changing onset dates, or an earlier denial of ringing, weighed against the veteran's account.
Separation paperwork where the veteran denied ear trouble was weighed against the claim

Nose, sinus or asthma conditions: a doctor said the condition worsens existing sleep apnea

hurt.text: Silent service records, a normal separation exam, and a diagnosis years after service
